narrative:
The model has analyzed your academic situation and determined that there’s a **13% chance** you might not pass your final year. While this isn’t a certainty—it’s a warning sign that the school is taking seriously. Because this probability exceeds a 10% threshold, you’ve been required to take remedial courses to help you stay on track.

The decision isn’t random—it’s based on three key factors that stood out in your profile. First, the model noticed that **why you chose this school** plays a role. Most students who don’t need extra support picked it for the course quality or because it was close to home, but your main reason was its reputation. While reputation isn’t a bad thing, it suggests you might not be as deeply connected to the school’s academic environment as others, which can sometimes affect focus.

Second, the model looked at how much time you spend studying each week. On average, students who don’t need remedial courses study between 2 to 5 hours, while you’re in the middle range—studying **5 to 10 hours**. While this is better than the lowest group, it’s still below what many high-performing students do. Small increases in study time could make a big difference in your confidence and performance.

Finally, the model checked your record of past failures. Unlike many students who haven’t struggled before, you’ve had **no prior failures**, which actually works in your favor—it shows you’re capable of improvement. However, the combination of the other two factors made the model cautious about your current trajectory.

This isn’t a reflection of your ability, but a chance to adjust and strengthen your approach. The remedial courses are designed to help you fill any gaps and build habits that will set you up for success. Focus on increasing your study time slightly, engage more with your school community, and use the extra support to refine your strategies. With these adjustments, you’ll be in a much stronger position to pass—and even excel—next year.
